ANKARA, Turkey, Feb. 2  (De- 


layed). —Sir Hughe Knatchbull- 
Hugessen,, British Ambassador to 


Turkey, went to the meeting of 


Prime Minister Churchill and Presi- 


dent Ismet Inonu of Turkey Satur- | 


day disguised as a hunter, it was 
disclosed today. 
The Ambassado® and his party 


took shotguns and hunting kits to) 


confuse any Axis agents who might 
have been lurking about. 

The envoy, on his return from the 
Adana conference, said today that 
Turkey was not “asked to enter the 
war” and German propaganda to 


this effect was a “complete fabrica- | 


tion.” The object of the conference, 
he said, was “to provide Turkey with 
more defensive armaments against 
the uncertainties of the future.” 
Nothing was signed at the confer- 


ence and the two leaders “didn't) 


decide if such and such a thing hap- 
pens Turkey will do such and such,” 
the British envoy added. 

“Turkey remains as free to make 
her own decisions as before,” he 


declared.

field, and a good bowler, or pitcher, 


it bounce every which way from the 
hheavy ground.

mammoth iron center of Magnitog- 
orsk, and the iron works there was 
begun as part of the program to es- 
tablish many major industries in 
the safety of the Urals.

ekin: . 
It may be difficult to picture, 
any link between plane and tank, 


but there’s one big tie that binds}. 


--the power turret—and it’s caus- 
ing plenty of difficulty for the) 
enemy. 
Although the power-operated 
gun mount hasn’t been heralded 
as much as our secret bombsight, 
it’s almost as potent and, if the 
bombsight is our No. 1 Axis- 
baffier, the power turret is cer- 
tainly No. 2 on the list coveted 
by the Nazis and Japs. 
Revolutionize Tactics ‘a 
With tank | 
warfare have been revolutionized: 
Bombers have been made virtually 
independent of fighter escorts; 
tanks have been. enabled to fire 
their guns in any direction, regard- 
less of their course. 
Here’s how the power turret has 
transformed the battleships of the 


@ir from vulnerable targets into 
self-protecting death-dealers: 
It overcomes the terrific force of 


the propellers’ slipstream, thus al-| 


_eontend with fighter planes travel- 


lowing the gunner steacy 
aim on his target. This steady aim. 
or “tracking”. is coupled with a 
sight so effective that it is almost 
hard to miss the attacking fighters. 

There is a variety of © sights. 
Ranging from the simple, nén-com- | 
puting reflector type to the com-- 
plex, computing sights which solve 
a@ number of air combat problems 
such as range, prediction, ballistics 
and others.

turrets was felt. 

Becatise of the slipstream force 
resulting from high speeds, it be- 
came impossible for a gunner to 
lean out of the cockpit and, with 
his ring-mounted machine gun, get 
a sieady aim on his target. 

Power turrets of today have to

ing 380 miles and more an hour; 
must, therefore, be operated 
a source of power other than 
manual, preferably electric or hy- 
Graulic. 

it was back in the early 1930's 
when, such turrets made their 
bow, But it wasn’t until the bat- 
tle, of Dunkerque that they _ 
proved their value in combat. 


In*a surprise appearance over 
the Dunkerque beaches, according 
to official announcements from 
the Royal Air Force, 12 Boulton 
Paul Defiants—one of the first

‘What startled the German air- 
men was,the they were shot 
down” while: mg parallel with 
and at presumably safe distances 
from the British aircraft—an oper- 
ation made possible only with 
power-operated turrets, of whieh | 
the Germans knew little. 


Eliminate Blind Spots 


Turrets are located on the ‘top 
and bottom of medium and heavy 
bombers, and some, like the Boeing 
Fortresses, carry another in the 
tail. This deadly armament, sup 
plemented with flexible waist, nose | 
and tail guns, offers such effec- | 
tive intersecting cones of fire that | 
“blind spots” are eliminated. Thus, | 
no matter from what angle enemy 
fighters approach they’re bound to. 
be met with plenty ef fire. 

The fire power not only enables 
a bomber to complete its mission 
and return to base, but permits :t 
to. invite combat with fighter 
planes—a case of the hunted be- 
coming the hunter. | 

And because it makes the bomb 
ers independent of fighter escorts, ,

it allows deeper sweeps into enemy) 
territory than would be possible 
with the escort of shorter-range_

Ask Rommel About Tanks 


On tanks, the man who could. 
best tell what the revolving turret | 
has accomplished is Field Marshal | 
Erwin Rommel, who has felt the 
power of the General Sherman’ 
tank, which is so equipped. 

Before the General Sherman, the 
army was using the General Grant 
tank, which had a rigid gun tur- 
ret that handicapped the gunner 
in that he could hit objects only 
in front—to draw a bead on a tar- 
get moving to the side, the whole 
tank had to be turned. 

Now with the electrically-oper- 
ated turret permitting the gunner 
to aim anywhere, no matter which 
way the tank is héaded, you've’ 
seen how it changed the whole) 
comple&amp;ion of the battle in Africa. 

One taste of its power, and Rom- 
mel was on his way—backward. 

So the relationship between 
Cousin Bomber and Cousin Tank— 
the power turret—if its not exactly 
a blood link, is at least a _—_- 
letting one.

[By the Associated Press] 

Feb. 8—The fall of Kursk, one of the principal 
bastions of the Berman 1971-47 Winter line, in a surprise 
Soviet offensive was announced tonight in a special Russian 
communique, marking a victory approaching in importance 
the Russian triumph at Stalingrad. 

As the crumbling of this northern pivot of the Nazi 
defense line was announced, pressure was increased on an- 
other of the key Nazi defenses — Rostov, gateway to the 
Caucasus, where the Russians are besieging the city from 
the south and another column is driving down from the north, 

Entire Nazi Defense Line Imperiled 

The capture of Kursk imperiled the entire German de- 
fensive line in Russia. 

The railroad city had been in German hands since No- 
vember 11, 1941, falling to the Nazis only four and a half 
months after they launched their drive into Russia. It was 
a main springboard of the German offensive last summer 
that swept to Voronezh and Stalingrad and overran sauch 
of the Caucasus. 


The Russian counter-offensive of last winter carried 
nearly to Kursk, but fell short of the city, where the Germans 
had built one of their strongest positions in all Russia.

Hoover 


Washington, Feb. 8 — Herbert 
Hoover declared today that “the 
size of the army must be modified, 
at least for the immediate period} 
of 1943,” and the armed forces 
should supply some of 1,000,000 ad- 


needed in farming and metal and 
oil industries. 

Hoover envisaged at least three 
more years of war, but observed: 

“Time runs in our favor. We do 
not, therefore, need try to do every- 
thing all at once. The knockout 
blow to Germany can be deliv- 
ered more contents in 1944 than in 
1943.” 

“Might Break” Home Front 

“It is a serious consideration that 

we might break the back of our 


internal degeneration, such as is 
now the fate of Germany. We 
should not imperil it by doing too 
much too fast. Especially when time 
runs in our favor.” 

(The House Military Committee 
is considering a bill to restrict the 


eral Senators, including Thomas 
(D., Okla.) and Bankhead (D., 
Ala.), have been discussing the ad- 
visability of limiting appropriations 
in order to hold down the number 
of men in the army and navy.) | 
Warns Of “Fatal Error” 

Remarking that theearmed forces 
intend to have. more than 11,000 
000 members by the end of 1943, 
the former President told a press 
conference: 

“If we attempt too much on the’ 
military side, we may commit the 
fatal error of overstraining.on the 
home front and thus damage our 
effectiveness in ultimate victory. 

~ Must Expect Long War | 

“There is a limit to our capacities 
and resources, great as they are. 
And in our planning we must, at 
least, prepare for a long war. 

“Including the defeat of Japan, 
we must envisage at least three 
more years of war, and a prudent 


nation would possibly envisage five 
years.”

New York, Feb, 9—Japanese Imperial headquarters announced today the withdrawal 
of Japanese-forces from Guadalcanal Island in the Solomons “after their missions had 
been fulfilléd,” the Berlin radio reported in a dispatch datelined Tokyo, 

The broadcast said the Japanese also announced the evacuation of the Buna‘ area in| 
New Guinea, apparently an admission, nearly three weeks. delayed,. of the destruction 
of the Jap army in Papua by General MacArthur’s American and Australian forces. 

Thus Tokyo admitted defeat of its ‘half-year effort to prevent complete American’ 
occupation of Guadalcanal. It was Japan’s first admission in this war of abandonment: 


of vital territory. The announcement put Japanese losses in the-two theaters at 16,734

Stalingrad, Feb. 9—Lieut. Gen. 
Vasily, Chuikov, commander of the 
Soviet Sixty-second Army which 
held Stalingrad, blew a cloud of 
smoke from his Russian cigarette 
toward the ceiling of the dugout. 

He considered the question: 
“What were the tactical mistakes 
of the Germans?” 

“The Germans made no tactical 
mistakes,” said the fighting com- 
mander who formerly was the Rus- 
sian military attache in China and 
adviser to China’s armies. 
“The Germans,” he: added 
thoughtfully, “made the strategic 
mistake of putting Hitler in com- 
mand.” —_— 

City The Main Factor 

“Was Stalingrad the main factor 
in the destruction of the German 
Sixth Army?” 

“Yes,” Chuikov replied. “The 
Sixth army could not break away. 
The (Russian) Sixty-second army 
held the Sixth until the other 
forces arrived.” 


| 


The general then estimated thatf- 


the Germans had lost 500,000 men 
in killed and captured in trying to 
take Stalingrad. 
' He disclosed that the Germans 
had reached the Volga. in two 
places, holding a total length of 
three an done-half miles of river 
bank; but Stalingrad sprawls for 
thirty miles along the west shore 
of the stream. The largest sector 
held by the Germans was the trac- 
tor works which American engi-

fight

close that “many times Germans

in each other’s arms in death.”

Both Chuguyev and Volchansk 
fell after sharp fighting, the Rus- 
sians said, and the Germans spoke 

of the front as “incoherent.” 
Seeking to explain the swift, sur- 
prise assaults which were bowling} 
over German bases one after the 
other in the Kharkov perimeter, a 
Berlin broadcast recorded by the 
Associated Press said abnormally 
heavy snowfalls all along the front 
from Orel to the Donets basin so 
reduced the range of German divi- 
- sions and hindered observation that 
the Russians frequently were able 
to slip through the Germans’ “thin 
line of bases and strongpoints.”

CAIRO, Feb. 10 (4).—General 
Sir Harold, Alexander, British 
commander in the Middle 
East, praised war correspondents 
today for their activities in th 
North African campaign. “Your 
work has been admirable both in 
stories and pictures,” he said. 
“You have been praised at home 
and abroad. On behalf of the 
Army, I wish to thank you very 
much indeed not only for your 


war system of trenches, barbed-wire 


and concrete pillboxes sixty-five 
miles inside the Tunisian border, 
but pointed out that it extends only 
forty miles into the desert. 

He then expressed his confidence 
that the line could be turned by 
sufficiently strong forces, which 
could swing around the end through 
hill. country much like that tra- 
versed into Tripoli. 

When the line was built by the 
French, he said, the engineers were 
not thinking of mobile forces such 
as have warred back and forth 
across the Libyan desert. 

Might Stand Near Gabes 

However, he expected Rommel 
would stay in that line as long as 
he was not threatened with being 
isolated in southern Tunisia, he 


said. 
When driven out, the Axis gen- 


work but for your wise discretion.”

BOMBAY; India, Feb. 10 (CP). 
The text of the statement issued 
today by the Indian government 
on Mohandas K. Gandhi’s hunger 
strike follows: 


M. K. Gandhi has informed the 
Viceroy he proposes to undertake 
a fast of three weeks’ duration 
from Feb. 10. It is to be a fast 
according to his capacity and dur- 
ing it Mr. Gandhi proposes to add 
the juices of citrus fruit to water, 
making the water drinkable, as 
his wish is not to fast to death, 
but to survive the ordeal. 

The government of India de- 
plore the use of the weapon of 
fasting to achieve political ends. 
There can, in their judgment, be 
no justification for it, and Mr. 
Gandhi has himself admitted in 
the past it contains an element of 
coercion. 

The government of India can 
‘nly express their regret Mr. 
Gandhi should think it necessary 
to.employ such a weapon on this 
occasion and should seek a jus- 
tification for it in anything which 
the government may have said or 
done in connection with the move“ 
ment initiated by him and his co: 
workers in the Congress party. 

The government of India have 
no intention on their part of al- 
lowing the fast to deflect their 
policy. Nor will they be respon- 
sible for its consequences on Mr! 
Gandhi’s health, They cannot pre- 
vent Mr. Gandhi from fasting. If 
was their wish, however, that, 
he decided to do so, he shoul 
do so as a free man and unde 
his own arrangements so as 
bring out clearly that responsi 
bility for any fast and its conse 
quences rested exclusively wit 
him. 


“At His Own Risk” 


They accordingly informed Mr, 
Gandhi he would be released for 
the purpose and for the duration 


dhi is not prepared to..take 
advantage of that fact and if he 
fasts while in detention he does so 
solely on his own responsibility 
and.at his own risk. 
He would be at liberty in that 
event to have his own medical at- 
tendants and also to receive visits 
from friends with permission of 
the government during its, (the 
fast). period. 
The government of India pro- 
poses to issue in.due course a full 
statement on the origin and de- 
velopment of the movement which 
was initiated last August and 
measures which it has been com- 
pelled to adopt to deal with it, 
but they think this is a suitable 
occasion for a brief review of 
events of the last few weeks. 

Mr. Gandhi in his *orrespond- 
ence with the Viceroy. had repudi- 
ated all responsibilty for the 
consequences flowed 
from the “Quit India’? demand 
which he and the Congress have 
put forward. 

This contention will not bear 
examination. Mr. Gandhi’s own 
statement 
was launched envisaged anarchy 
as an alternative to the existing 


‘Jorder and referfed to the struggle 


as a “fight to the finish in the 
course of which he would not hesi- 
tate to fun any risk however 
great.” 

“An Open Rebellion” 


As much has been made of his 
offer to meet the Viceroy, it is nec- 
essary to point out that at a press 
interview July 14, after the Con- 
gress working committee resolu- 
tion was passed, Mr. Gandhi stated 
there was no room left in the pro- 
posal for withdrawal or negotia- 
tion; there was no question of one 
more chance; after all, it was an 
open rebellion which was to be as 
short and swift as possible. _. 

His last message was: “Do or 
die.”

Reviewed Tripoli Divisions 

Here I found General Mont- 
gomery. 
_ I must confess I didn’t realize 
how magnificent a city and har- 
bor Tripoli had been made. It is 
the first Italian city to be deliv- 
ered by British arms from the 
grip of the Hun. Naturally there 
was lively enthusiasm among the 
Italian people. I can hardly do. 
justice to the effusiveness of 
demonstrations of which I was 
the fortunate object. I had the 


honor, as servant, to review 


two of our forward divisions. 

The 5ist Highland Division is 
the successor of that brave divi- 
sion that was overwhelmed on 
the coasts of France in the trage- 
dies of 1940. 

‘It has more than equalized the 
account which Scotland has 
opened in this matter.

Washington, Feb. 11—A_possi- 
bility that Mme. Chiang Kai-shek 
would be invited to. outline China’s 
lend-lease needs developed today 
as the House Foreign Affairs Com- 
mittee continued its study of ex- 
tending the mutual aid act for an- 
other year. 

Representative Curley, 
Democratic Governor of Massachu- 
setts, said he would ask the House 
to invite the American-educated 
wife of the Chinese generalissimo 
to appear “if she has an woppor- 
tunity to do so.” 

10 P. C. Of All Aid Urged 

Curley earlier this week intro- 
duced a measure to allocate to 
China ten per cent. of al! Jend- 
lease aid, arguing that it would 
save more than 500,000 American 
lives and enable the Chinese to de- 
feat the Japanese in six months. 

The House, learning that Mad- 
ame Chiang would be in the Capi- 
‘Ital next week, already has ar- 


ranged an informal reception: simi- 
lar to those accorded the rulers 
and nobility of other nations. 

The idea of obtaining her views 


[By the Associated Pregsi. 


on lend-lease won instant support} 


from Representative Mansfield (D., 
Mont.), Foreign Affairs Committee 
member, who has argued frequent- 
ly for increased aid to China. 

“It is a wonderful opportunity,” 
he exclaimed. “I can think of no 
one in this country better qualified 
to discuss China’s needs.” 

Both spokcsmen for the lendq- 
lease administration and Secretary 
of the Navy Frank Knox have ex- 
pressed regret that aid to China has 
not reached greater proportions, 
but they emphasize the difficulties} 
in making deliveries since the clos- 
ing of the Burma road. 

Curley and Mansfield advocate 
cargo planes, but officials point out | 
that gasoline supplies pose a prob-| 
lem there,

really mean by that and you will 
' get what, on the surface, may

One will say he is fighting for 
the right to say what he pleases 
and to read and listen to what 
he likes. 

Another will say he is fight- 
ing because he never wants to 
see the Nazi swastika flying 
over the First Baptist Church on 
Elm Street. 

Another soldier will say he is 
fighting for the right to work 
and earn three square meals a 
day for himself and his folks. 

A fourth soldier will say he is 
fighting in this world war so 
that his children and grandchil- 
dren will not have to go back to 
Europe, or Africa, or Asia, to do 
this ugly job all over again. 

But all these answers really 
add up to the same thing: Every 
American fights for freedom. 
| And today the personal freedom 
of every American and his fam- 
ily depends, and in the future 
will increasingly depend, upon 
the freedom of his neighbors in 
other lands. 

For today the whole world is 
one neighborhood. That is why 
this war, which had its begin- 
nings in seemingly remote areas, 
' has spread to every continent 
_ and most of the islands of the 
_ sea, involving the lives and the 
| liberties of the entire human 
race. And unless the peace that 
follows recognizes that the whole 
world is one neighborhood and 
does justice to the whole human 
race, the germs of another world 
war will remain as a constant 
threat to mankind. 


Tells of Soldiers’ Worries 


I talked with many people in 
our armed forces—along the 
coast and through the islands of 
the Western Hemisphere and up 
the coast of West Africa. Many 
of our soldiers and sailors were 
concerned about the state of the 
home front. They receive all 
kinds of exaggerated reports and 
rumors that there is too much 
complaining here at home and 
too little recognition of the 
realities of war; that selfish 


labor leaders are threatening to 
call strikes which would greatly 
curtail the output of our war in-

rationing and priorities; and
